newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir relief craft to blast off Saturday.
newsitem.headline: Mir relief craft to blast off Saturday.

text.p: A Progress spacecraft carrying an emergency repair kit for the crippled Mir orbital station will blast off from Russia's Baikonur cosmodrome on Saturday.

The supplies aboard the unmanned Progress M-35 include oxygen, food and water for the Russian-American crew as well as the tools needed to repair Mir after it lost up to half its electric power in a collision on June 25.

The craft, due to be launched at 0411 GMT, should reach Mir on Monday, but the three men on board the station still face a long and uncomfortable wait of nearly two weeks before attempting risky electrical repairs during a spacewalk.

As Americans celebrated Independence Day holiday by landing their Pathfinder probe on Mars, their former rivals in the Cold War space race were battling, now with NASA help, to keep Russia's contribution to space exploration alive.

Mission Control officials said the Mir repairs -- vital if the ageing station is not to be abandoned -- were put back by a week to July 17-18 to allow the two Russian cosmonauts more time to practise the delicate manoeuvres they will have to perform during a spacewalk in bulky suits in cramped conditions.

Mission Control was also struggling to fix a malfunction in the gyroscopic systems that keep Mir's energy-giving solar panels properly lined up to the Sun as it hurtles round the Earth in orbit. In their absence, the cosmonauts are firing their rocket engines periodically.

Officials hoped to sort out this problem by the time the Progress caft blasts off. Mission Control said the gyroscope trouble would not affect a docking with Progress on Monday, but experts say the overall lack of power on Mir will make the operation problematic.

It was during a practice docking manoeuvre with another Progress cargo craft on June 25 that the Spektr module, one of half a dozen components now making up the 11-year-old station, was holed and one of four solar panels on it was smashed.
Officials have declined to confirm or deny a Russian newspaper report that investigators held Mir commander Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, responsible for the collision.
Only split-second reactions saved the crew from suffocation as air hissed out into space. But in sealing off the Spektr they were forced to sever the power supply from the undamaged panels.

The supplies on the new Progress include a special airtight plate which Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39, will fit into the door of the Spektr module to feed 10 electric cables back into the main station.
Fellow cosmonauts at the Zvyozdny Gorodok (Star City) training centre near Moscow are testing the manoeuvres in bulky spacesuits in a submerged mock-up of Mir.

While the two Russians attempt to rewire the ship in clumsy gloves, British-born NASA physicist Michael Foale, 40, will sit in a spacesuit in the Soyuz escape capsule, ready to read out instructions to his colleagues during the operation. The Soyuz is the crew's lifeboat if things go wrong.
Officials insist the cosmonauts are in no immediate danger and are in good spirits despite the inactivity, heat and darkness enforced by the lack of power.
Russian officials are far from giving up on Mir yet. Deputy mission director Viktor Blagov said a relief crew, including a Frenchman, was still preparing for a launch in August.
For the three men now on board, the most welcome part of the latest cargo may be parcels from home. Foale lost most of his kit in Spektr and has asked NASA to send him a new toothbrush.
